items.action: Quays served as meeting points where goods arrived and left; cargo of people and goods went by river to Santarém, Vila Franca de Xira and Lisbon.
items.place: cais na Barquinha; Santarém, Vila Franca de Xira, Lisboa

items.action: Upriver products were unloaded at those ports; boats returned with varied goods to Barquinha, where animal-drawn carts took them on to other territories.
Boats traded up and down the river, carrying forest wealth, ice from Lousã and Estrela mountains and farm produce, returning with salt, cloth and paper.
items.cargo: forest products, ice from serras da Lousã e da Estrela, fruits of the land, salt
items.who: gentes de riba Tejo, Beiras and Alentejo

items.action: Vila Nova da Barquinha remembers a glorious time when its fragatas sailed the Tagus down to the Mar da Palha or the open sea.
items.place: Vila Nova da Barquinha, Mar da Palha

items.action: The arrais or master of the vessel is portrayed as a symbol of the Tagus, knowing the river's secrets and forecasting weather by the stars without instruments.
An examination licence was issued to António Farinha of Barquinha to serve as arrais of a boat owned by Manuel Farinha, with certification from the Arsenal's patrão-mor.
items.conditions: obliged to answer to the almotacés and follow the mesa's orders
items.place: rio de Lisboa e riba Tejo
items.who: António Farinha; Manuel Farinha; patrão-mor João dos Santos

items.action: All maritime and river activity was governed by municipal ordinances (posturas) setting rights and duties of boat masters and conduct of people at landing places and river ports.
Almotacés oversaw commercial acts, enforced price tables, fined breaches of the posturas and could detain offenders; privileged persons only if caught in the act.
items.conditions: privileged persons detained only in flagrante delito

items.action: The river stretch in front of Barquinha had several quays: Barquinha, Hidráulica, Jacinta and Vapor; the existence of a 'Vapor' quay remains a puzzle.
items.place: Barquinha: cais da Barquinha, da Hidráulica, da Jacinta, do Vapor

items.action: Overland trade was hard: no reasonable roads linked municipalities, so goods moved by ox-drawn carts and wagons to the river ports of the riba Tejo.
A real road network began to be built; around then river transport dominated, up and down between Vila Velha de Rodão, Abrantes, Barquinha, Santarém, Vila Franca and Lisbon.
items.place: Vila Velha de Rodão, Abrantes, Barquinha, Santarém, Vila Franca, Lisboa

items.action: Government pushed road and rail networks to integrate markets; trains, motor traffic and steam navigation were seen as ending isolation of villages.
Road network grew from 1106 km of ordinary roads in 1858 to 2195 km in 1865, about 4000 km in 1874 and 13,000 km in 1900.
The first railway line was inaugurated; the Companhia Real dos Caminhos de Ferro Portugueses was formed in 1863, reaching Elvas, and the train advanced further in 1864.
items.who: Companhia Real dos Caminhos de Ferro Portugueses

items.action: Railway reached Alentejo-Lisbon coast link in 1864 and Algarve in 1865, beginning the rail competition with river transport.
Rail network grew from 701 km in 1865 to 1299 km in operation by 1882, with Beira Alta line reaching Vilar Formoso.
Another 1000 km of railway were built between 1882 and 1894, and the railway began to dominate transport.
Faster road transport in the first quarter of the 20th century put river traffic's dominance into crisis.
Dams were built on the Tejo and the Zêzere in the 1950s, further hindering river navigation.
Sawmills of Manuel Viera da Cruz & Filhos and Tomaz da Cruz & Filhos at Praia do Ribatejo declined; they had employed about 500 workers.
items.who: Manuel Viera da Cruz & Filhos Lda; Tomaz da Cruz & Filhos

items.action: Timber used to float down the Zêzere bed to Praia do Ribatejo; after the dams it no longer travelled on the river.
The sawmill firms sued the Portuguese State for lost profits caused by the dams; the lawsuit was filed by Dr. Azeredo Perdigão and failed.
Port activity at Barquinha declined due to rail and road alternatives, dams and recurring silting of the Tejo.
Passenger transport used the catraio, caíque, bote, batel and canoa.
Cargo was carried by mill boats, Riba-Tejo boats, bateiras, faluas, varinos-avieiros and fragatas.
items.boat: barcos de moinhos, barcos de Riba-Tejo, bateiras, faluas, va

items.action: Fishing used picareto, abrangel, catrafúcio (three-plank boat), saveiros and muletas.
items.boat: picareto, abrangel, catrafúcio ou barco de três tábuas, save

items.action: Varinos-avieiros and fragatas were the most representative cargo boats of the Tejo.
All navigation was then done by sail and oars.
Law of 24 November 1837 by Queen Maria II regulated steam vessels on the Tejo and opened a concession tender.
Notice of 4 August 1851 set terms for a 15-year exclusive concession of Tejo steam navigation, requiring daily services on northern routes.
items.conditions: beyond canal mouth only for boats drawing under four feet
items.place: Alhandra, Vila Franca de Xira, Carregado, Foz do Canal d'Azambuja

items.action: On 25 July 1862 a vessel carried a steam locomotive upriver to the Barquinha steam quay, requiring large excavations there.
A photo shows a varino carrying tonnes of cork upriver; another shows people, animals and a cart boarding.
First steam passenger service on the Tagus between Lisbon and Santarém began, but the voyage ended at Alqueidão because silting of the river prevented going further.
items.boat: steam vessel with wooden hull and 20 NHP engine, built at Mo
items.conditions: silting of the Tagus stopped the route at Alqueidão
items.gear: steam engine by Fawcett, Littledale & Co.
items.who: Companhia/service ordered by Portugal's consul-general in Liverpool, António Jul

items.action: Steam vessel built in Liverpool was reportedly the first steamship ordered by a foreign state, first to cross the Bay of Biscay and first to call at Portuguese ports.
items.place: Liverpool, Bay of Biscay, Portuguese ports

items.action: In the 1850s intercontinental transport relied on sailing ships, but mass emigration of European workers to America became chiefly the age of steamships.
items.boat: sailing ships of 200 to 400 tonnes; steamships

items.action: Steamers cut the Lisbon to Rio de Janeiro crossing from about six weeks under sail to three weeks, or two weeks without stops.
Ships entering the Tagus mouth were counted, excluding fishing boats: more sailing ships than steamers.
Boats of various sizes and shapes sailed between Lisbon and points along the Tagus.
items.boat: barcos de diversos tamanhos e feitios

items.action: Registered avieiro boats were counted at Abrantes and Barquinha, described as thriving Middle Tagus ports.
Almeida Garrett describes a steamer passenger trip from Santarém to Lisbon, nearly empty yet slow, arriving at Terreiro do Paço around five in the afternoon.
items.place: Santarém to Lisbon, Terreiro do Paço

items.action: Alexandre Herculano records a steamer journey upriver from Lisbon, via riverside towns to the Azambuja canal mouth, then onward by carriage to Santarém.
items.place: Lisbon, Alverca, Alhandra, Vila Franca, Vila Nova, Azambuja canal mouth, Santaré

items.action: Travellers from Lisbon often changed boats, going by steamer to a place such as Vila Franca or Santarém, then taking a sailing boat upstream.
Steam passenger service between Lisbon and the Azambuja canal mouth ceased by decree because of heavy losses to the company, after the railway opened.
items.conditions: railway line opened east of Lisbon to Virtudes station
items.place: Lisbon, Alhandra, Vila Franca de Xira, Carregado, Vila Nova da Rainha, Azambuja

items.action: Chartered steam cargo boats, not passenger boats, from Lisbon moored at the Cais do Vapor in Barquinha, obliged to make a return voyage.
The Prado paper mill had warehouses beside the steam quay on the east side of Barquinha town, so goods often arrived and left there.
items.place: cais do vapor, Rua da Barca, Barquinha

items.action: The Prado paper mill began operating in the early 1820s at Prado, parish of Pedreira, municipality of Tomar.
The Prado paper mill was sold to a group of businessmen by João de Oliveira Casquilho and his brother-in-law Henrique de Roure Pietra.
items.who: João de Oliveira Casquilho; Henrique de Roure Pietra

items.action: The Prado and Marianaia mills made writing, foolscap and wrapping papers from rags and wool, which required a warehouse at the Barquinha steam quay.
items.who: fábricas do Prado e da Marianaia

items.action: Shipments of unspecified wool fabrics from Belgium and England, brought by steamboat, were stored in the Barquinha warehouse to be processed.
items.cargo: tecidos de lã da Bélgica e da Inglaterra

items.action: Goods were moved from the warehouse onto ox carts and taken along the macadam district road no. 51 to the paper mills.
items.place: Barquinha to paper mills, estrada distrital n.º 51 (estrada de neveiros)

items.action: The railway reached the area; steamboats gradually stopped docking at Barquinha's steam quay and the Prado warehouses fell into disuse.
Engineer Manuel José Júlio Guerra published proposals for works on the Tagus riverbed and towpaths to improve navigation and protect adjacent fields; they were not carried out.
Alexandre Herculano, royal commissioner inventorying convent archives, began his journey at the port of Barquinha and travelled onward on horseback.
Snow was collected in wells on the Lousã mountain and carried by cart to Barquinha, as Herculano noted in 1853.
items.conditions: snow 14 feet deep in the hollow that February
